shots.title: Where Internet Lives
shots.vo: Okay so. You probably think this video reached you through a satellite. Nope.

shots.label: Intercontinental Data
shots.sub: Travels through cables on the seabed
shots.vo: More than 95 percent of the data crossing between continents travels through cables lying on the bottom of the ocean.

shots.title: The Cloud Is In *The Sea*
shots.vo: The cloud lives in the sea. And out in the deep water, the cable carrying it is about as thick as a garden hose.

shots.say: What if someone cuts them all?
shots.title: The Vulnerability
shots.vo: So what if every single one got cut? And the weirder question: why hasn't it happened already?

shots.title: Local Roads vs Oceanic Bridges
shots.vo: Think of the internet as a planet of cities. Inside your country, data drives around on local roads.

shots.title: Only So Many Bridges
shots.sub: Crossing oceans requires undersea physical links
shots.vo: But to reach another continent it has to cross the sea, and there are only so many bridges.

shots.title: Traffic Comparison
shots.vo: Satellites exist. They're the helicopters. Great for remote places, terrible for moving a whole city's traffic.

shots.title: Not Scalable
shots.vo: Nobody commutes by helicopter. Well. Some billionaires.

shots.label: Around The Earth
shots.vo: There are roughly five to six hundred of these bridges, about 1.4 million kilometers of cable. Enough to wrap around the Earth about thirty-five times,

shots.title: Invisible Lifeline
shots.vo: and almost nobody has ever seen one.

shots.title: Flashing Across Oceans
shots.vo: Here's how it works. Inside the hose are hair-thin strands of glass. Your message becomes pulses of laser light flashing across an entire ocean.

shots.title: Undersea Architecture
shots.vo: Every so often a repeater, a little box on the seabed, boosts the signal so it doesn't fade.

shots.title: The Cable Landing Station
shots.vo: On each coast, the cable crawls up a beach into a plain building called a landing station, which looks like the place you'd go to renew a fishing licence.

shots.label: Undersea Breaks
shots.vo: Which sounds sturdy. Until you learn cables break around 150 to 200 times a year.

shots.title: Actual Cable Culprits
shots.vo: Not mostly from spies. Mostly from fishing gear and ship anchors dragging across the seabed.

shots.title: Deep Sea Hazards
shots.vo: Sharks have reportedly bitten them too, and Google reportedly wrapped some cables in extra protective material,

shots.title: Shark Mitigation
shots.sub: An actual agenda item in tech boardroom meetings
shots.vo: which means someone in a meeting had to say 'shark mitigation' with a straight face.

shots.title: The Internet *Reroutes*
shots.vo: So why didn't your Wi-Fi notice? Because the internet reroutes. Routers constantly gossip using a system called BGP,

shots.title: Dynamic Fallback
shots.vo: basically 'hey, I can reach Singapore, send stuff through me.' When a cable dies, traffic takes the next-best path. Slower, more crowded, but it arrives.

shots.title: The Fragile Limit
shots.vo: Here's the wild part though. Rerouting only works if there's somewhere else to go. And one country found out what happens when there isn't. We'll get there.

shots.title: Repair Sequence
shots.vo: Because the twist is, the cables aren't the scariest part. The fixing is. A repair ship sails out, drags a grappling hook along the seabed, fishes up the cable and splices it on deck.

shots.label: Global Repair Fleet
shots.sub: Takes days to weeks per break
shots.vo: That can take days to weeks. And there are reportedly only a few dozen of these ships for the whole planet.

shots.title: Historical Outages
shots.vo: Real outages show the pattern. In 2006, an earthquake off Taiwan damaged several cables at once and parts of Asia crawled. In 2008, cuts in the Mediterranean slowed the internet across Egypt, the Middle East and India.

shots.title: Red Sea 2024
shots.sub: A drifting abandoned anchor took out regional connectivity
shots.vo: In 2024, Red Sea cables were damaged, reportedly by the dragging anchor of a ship that had been attacked and abandoned.

shots.title: 1929 Avalanche
shots.vo: Nerd bonus: in 1929, an earthquake off Newfoundland triggered an underwater avalanche, and scientists later worked out its speed from the times each telegraph cable snapped.

shots.title: Telegraph Stopwatch
shots.vo: The internet's ancestors died as a stopwatch.

shots.title: Total Cable Severance
shots.vo: So, all of them cut at once? Your local internet mostly keeps running. But anything hosted abroad, cloud services, lots of apps, international payments, starts failing.

shots.title: Hundreds Is *A War*
shots.sub: A handful of ships cannot fix a worldwide collapse
shots.vo: Satellites carry a trickle. And with a few dozen ships facing hundreds of breaks, repairs take months. That's why it hasn't happened. One anchor is an accident. Hundreds is a war.

shots.label: Tonga Island Outage
shots.sub: 100k people cut off after volcano eruption
shots.vo: Remember the country with nowhere to reroute? In January 2022, an underwater volcano erupted near Tonga and severed its only international cable.

shots.title: Dark To The World
shots.vo: A nation of about a hundred thousand people went almost dark to the world, while families abroad waited to hear if relatives were okay. It took around five weeks to restore.

shots.title: Big Tech Underwriting
shots.vo: So here's my take. The real risk isn't sharks, and it's not a movie villain cutting everything. It's that plenty of places hang on one or two cables, and the planet's repair capacity is a handful of ships. Tech giants like Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon now fund a growing share of new cables.

shots.title: The Real Priority
shots.sub: The internet is only as global as its least connected place
shots.vo: Fine. But backup routes for small countries and more repair ships should be a priority, because the internet is only as global as its least connected place.

shots.title: Where Your Photos Live
shots.vo: So next time someone says your photos are in the cloud, correct them gently. They're in a garden hose on the ocean floor, next to a shark, waiting for a ship that's probably busy.

shots.title: If The Cable *Holds*
shots.vo: Subscribe, and if the cable holds, I'll see you in the next one.
